extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of mass communication and media studies
extracted.subtask_description: Use the Hierarchy of Influences (HOI) theoretical framework to analyze factors shaping news and media content across multiple nested levels, from macro social systems to individual journalists. The framework informs research design (treating content as the dependent variable) and comparative studies of journalism culture, routines, and organizational structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media content as dependent variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological stance: treat media content as the dependent variable influenced by factors located in the hierarchical framework rather than treating content as an independent variable (as in many media effects studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the five HOI levels as potential independent variables when designing studies; frame research questions to explain variation in content by locating influences at different hierarchical levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social systems (macro) influences
rubrics_metrics.description: The outermost level representing influences from social systems as a whole, focusing on how ideological forces shape and influence media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ this level especially in cross-national or comparative studies to account for broad cultural, ideological, political, and systemic factors that constrain or shape media content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social institutions (trans-organizational) influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Influences coming from the larger trans-organizational media field: how media organizations combine into institutions and become part of structured relationships that compete or depend on each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze inter-organizational relations, market and institutional pressures, norms of the field, and dependencies between media organizations when attributing influence at this level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media organizations (organizational/occupational) influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational level describing larger organizational and occupational context such as organizational policy, occupational roles, and how the media enterprise itself is structured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine newsroom policies, ownership, hierarchy, job roles, resources, and internal procedures that shape what content is produced and how; distinguish these organizational influences from individual routines and broader institutional forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine practices (work-process) influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Routines level: the daily practices and patterns (routines) developed by journalists that constrain and enable communicators; routines derive from audiences, organizations, and suppliers of content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider standard reporting practices, norms for covering beats, gatekeeping behaviors, sourcing practices, and constraints from audience expectations, organizational workflows, and content suppliers when assessing influence at this level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuals (micro) influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual communicator characteristics (personal and professional) located at the center of the model; attributes like gender, race, religion, political background, attitudes, values, roles, and education influence media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how journalists' personal backgrounds, ethical values, professional identities, and individual decisions shape content directly or indirectly via their roles and routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-level interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: The framework emphasizes that influence at one level may interact with influence at another level rather than operating in isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analysis, account for interactions and mediations between levels (e.g., how organizational policy mediates the effect of institutional pressures, or how individual values interact with routines); avoid attributing effects solely to a single level without considering nested influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research applicability and domains of use
rubrics_metrics.description: HOI has been used as a theoretical framework to study professionalism, journalistic roles, cross-national comparative studies, and news production processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the HOI to questions about journalism culture, differences across countries (e.g., Worlds of Journalism study), professionalism, and trust in institutions; use it to structure interview guides, comparative designs, and analyses that map influences onto the five levels.
